title.rendered: Understanding Past Realities of the Holocaust: Photography Versus Art

content.rendered: The Holocaust and the United Nations Outreach Programme, the Fritz Ascher Society for Persecuted, Ostracized and Banned Art, and the Permanent Mission of Germany to the United Nations organize a discussion marking the November Pogrom of 1938, euphemistically called “Kristallnacht.” Historians Dr. Christoph Kreutzmüller and Dr. Rachel Perry examine how photography and art depicted the Nazi state-orchestrated campaign of terror perpetrated against Jewish men, women, and children across Germany, Austria, and the Sudetenland from November 9 to 10, 1938. The discussion considers what photography and art reveal about the lived realities of the victims and the broader society in which the violence was perpetrated.

title.rendered: Media Bias in the United States: The Catastrophic Failure of Modern Journalism

content.rendered: Chai Mitzvah hosts David, U.S. Media Research Manager at CAMERA, for a presentation on how media institutions have failed to deliver quality journalism in their coverage of Israel. Drawing on his work at the media monitoring organization, David examines how such failures have vilified victims, left perpetrators unaccountable, and distorted policy debates. This is Part 1 of CAMERA’s three-part series on media bias in the U.S., U.K., and Israel.

title.rendered: More Than a Symbol: The Jewish Labor Bund in History

content.rendered: The YIVO Institute for Jewish Research hosts Joshua Meyers for a talk on the Jewish Labor Bund, drawing on the Bund Archive preserved at YIVO. The session traces the Bund’s history from its origins through World War II, when it served as the standard bearer of Diaspora Socialism in the Jewish communities of Eastern Europe, and examines its evolving relationships with Zionists, Communists, and other movements. The talk also considers the legacy of the Bund and of Diaspora Socialism in the 21st century.

title.rendered: The Pin That Slew the Serpent: Unearthing the Objects of the Talmud

content.rendered: The Community Scholar Program offers a course on everyday objects in the Talmudic text, from Hillel’s skylight to the hairpin of Rabbi Akiva’s daughter. While texts reflect the interests of the literate elite, objects such as furniture, clothes, and kitchenware open a window into the lives of the illiterate masses. The course explores how the rabbis used ordinary household items to respond to the concerns of society at large.

A book signing and light reception follow the program.

title.rendered: The Sound of Resistance: A Conversation with Author Heather Morris

content.rendered:
Heather Morris’s 2018 novel, “The Tattooist of Auschwitz” became an instant bestseller after it was published. Now, Morris returns with a new novel showcasing the astonishing bravery of ordinary people in extraordinary times.

In “The Pianist of Montparnasse,” Morris tells the story of 11-year-old Josephine and the teacher who risked everything for her. When Josephine’s mother and brother are arrested by the Nazis, her mother orders her to go to the only person she can trust: her piano teacher, Andrée Levallois. What Josie does not know is that her teacher and her parents are part of the French Resistance. Andrée and her parents take the child in, risking everything to keep her safe. But the stakes grow higher as their operations become more dangerous, and the family’s strength of will and conviction are tested as they fight for the future they hope to see.

Please join us to meet Heather Morris and discuss the book on Sunday November 1, 2026, 6 pm ET, online.
Sign up below to participate. You’ll receive a reminder email with a Zoom link before the event begins.
About our speakers:
Heather Morris is a native of New Zealand, now residing in Australia. For several years, while working in a large public hospital in Melbourne, she studied and wrote screenplays. In 2003, she was introduced to a gentleman who had “a story worth telling,” which formed the basis of her first novel, The Tattooist of Auschwitz, and its follow-up, Cilka’s Journey. Her third novel, Three Sisters, concluded the Tattooist trilogy. One of the twenty-first century’s best-selling books, The Tattooist of Auschwitz was made into an acclaimed miniseries in 2024. Heather’s books have sold more than nineteen million copies worldwide.
Heather will be in conversation with Rebecca Phillips, publisher of 70 Faces Media. 70 Faces Media is the organization behind six of the Jewish world’s most beloved and longstanding digital brands: JTA, My Jewish Learning, Kveller, The Nosher, Hey Alma, and the New York Jewish Week.
This conversation with Heather Morris is presented by Blackstone Publishing, our sponsor for the event.

title.rendered: The Odds of Light: Rabbi Noa Kushner

content.rendered:
Folio Literary Series: Wednesday, December 2 at 6 p.m. ET
When the world is at its darkest, that’s when to reach for light.

Sometimes, we’re lucky and light easily comes our way. Other times, we have to go out and search for it, or even make light for ourselves. Hanukkah is the holiday about people who, even against great odds, repeatedly refused to give up on the light.Rabbi Noa Kushner wrote Pretend You Believe for anyone who refuses to sit in the dark. If you are interested in what it means to claim light, for yourself and for this world, come and hear from this singular rabbi, who has brought tens of thousands of people closer to Jewish tradition through beautiful Shabbatot in San Francisco.

Noa will be in conversation with Andrew Silow-Carroll, Editor at Large, 70 Faces Media.
 
About Rabbi Noa Kushner:
Rabbi Noa Kushner is the founding rabbi of The Kitchen, a synagogue and institute in San Francisco whose approach to religion has become a model for communities worldwide. Devoted to religious access for all and committed to the beauty and depth of the tradition, The Kitchen is widely regarded as a way forward for Jewish and religious life today. Called a “measure of hope” in Haaretz and a “rabbi to watch” in Newsweek, Kushner has translated religious experiences and ideas for tens of thousands across the United States, Israel, and Paris.
